item.title: Burning the Bridge: Agentification and Domestic Value Added
item.description: arXiv:2611.31518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Firms that replace local work with foreign AI agents can produce more per paid hour while generating less income at home. We study this trade-off in a small open economy where exporters and local services both use agents. Once wages reach a reservation floor, extending agent use in local services lowers domestic income at unchanged foreign costs. Value added at constant prices and consumption also fall if suppliers capture enough of the saving. Exporters have an offset: adopting agents can expand production and earn the foreign exchange needed to pay for them. The difference is substantial. Using Brazilian accounts as a reference, a supplier bargaining share above about 0.15 is sufficient to make further local-service adoption reduce value added even at negligible foreign costs. The corresponding threshold in tradables is about 0.66. We derive separate export-growth requirements for preserving income and consumption and illustrate them using historical accounts for Brazil and Mexico. Cheaper agents ease the consumption requirement; lower export prices raise it. Over time, declining domestic capabilities can also make returning to local production more expensive, allowing suppliers to charge more at renewal.
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Levy Yeyati

item.title: The Effect of Remote Working on Regional Waste: Evidence from South Korea
item.description: arXiv:2611.31860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Remote working, or work-from-home (WFH), has become common around the world. However, its broader effects on social welfare, including waste generation, remain understudied. This study examines the impact of remote work on regional waste production in South Korea, using the COVID-19 pandemic as a natural experiment. Overall household waste changed little, but regions with greater WFH eligibility saw increases in plastic and textile waste and a decrease in food waste. These findings suggest that remote work may change consumption patterns and daily routines. Understanding these effects can help inform sustainable work practices and waste management as remote work becomes more widespread.
item.dc:creator: Hyoungchul Kim, Hee-Seung Yang

item.title: Grokipedia stretches the US political spectrum
item.description: arXiv:2611.32420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models now write reference works that people and other AI systems consult. Grokipedia, written by xAI's model, presents itself as a less biased alternative to crowd-edited Wikipedia. We compare the biographies of 1,614 Democratic and Republican current and former politicians, from Andrew Jackson to members of the current Congress, on both encyclopedias in February and November 2026. For nine in ten Republicans, Grokipedia's biography reads as if written by a more conservative author than Wikipedia's. For Democrats, this holds only about half the time. We find the politicians' ideology explains this asymmetry. For 1,022 politicians with Congressional roll call voting records, how conservative the author seems rises linearly with the politician's ideology and about twice as steeply on Grokipedia as on Wikipedia. Republicans in races where Elon Musk's America PAC spent money show no extra bias. Rather than favoring a party, Grokipedia stretches the political spectrum, moving the biographies of the most liberal politicians further left and of the most conservative politicians further right.
item.dc:creator: Philipp Koch, Alexander Posztos

item.title: Training decision models for simulating human respondents
item.description: arXiv:2611.31613v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as synthetic respondents in market research, conjoint analysis, and randomized experiments. However, synthetic choice data from off-the-shelf generative LLMs bias downstream econometric inference. Neither proprietary models nor higher reasoning effort reliably reduces this bias. We investigate decision models (System One architectures) for silicon sampling. Using choice training, we update KEV model weights on historical respondent-level choice microdata by conditional maximum likelihood, before inference and without target-study data. Across three model scales, training on two discrete choice experiments lowers treatment-effect error by 22% to 89% on four held-out studies from new domains (vaccines, nutrition labels, consumer rights, and AI) and new response formats. A small choice-trained model outperforms a much larger off-the-shelf model on three of the four studies. Although training on single studies lowers cross-entropy, it can exacerbate treatment-effect error. Choice training thus complements post-inference calibration by providing a stronger starting point for estimating human preferences.
item.dc:creator: Davood Wadi, Yu Ma

item.title: Decision support framework for mitigating failure demand in healthcare
item.description: arXiv:2611.32139v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Failure demand studies in healthcare are, by nature, observational field studies conducted by social scientists. Historically, these practices have neglected any follow-on analysis by economists, data analysts, or mathematicians. In this paper, we argue that the mitigation of failure demand can only be effectively navigated through analytical cost-benefit modelling conducted in conjunction with a comprehensive uncertainty-sensitivity analysis. Using an existing failure demand field study as the starting point, we demonstrate how such a follow up analysis can be conducted and formulate a pragmatic decision support methodological framework that can be disseminated to the researchers and practitioners throughout the broad healthcare field. The framework emanates from classical cost-benefit modelling that is then supplemented with Monte Carlo simulation in combination with the groundbreaking Simulation Decomposition (SimDec) method. The SimDec results reveal additional insights critical for decision making that could not be readily uncovered by any other existing techniques. While SimDec's methodological framework is straightforward to implement using various open-source computer code packages, this paper shows how non-technical healthcare practitioners can easily conduct an entirely congruent analysis via the freely-accessible web dashboard interface or the downloadable spreadsheet template.
item.dc:creator: Katariina Timonen, Mariia Kozlova, Roman Stepanov, Julian Scott Yeomans

item.title: Worth the Wait? How Response Time and Streaming Shape Judgments of Generative AI Answers and Chatbot Engagement
item.description: arXiv:2611.33050v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Answers from generative AI chatbots built on large language models (LLMs) now arrive at very different speeds: reasoning models deliberate before replying, while response caches can return a stored answer at once. Blind preference votes, which rank these models, are read as judgments of their text, and if delivery matters, faster answers are expected to gain. Research on the labor illusion and on how text appears on screen suggests instead that an answer which unfolds as it is written is credited over the same answer shown at once. We test these accounts with three sources of variation in natural use. First, compar:IA, a French government chatbot arena, answered repeated prompts, by a random draw, either with a fresh answer streamed as it was written or with a stored earlier answer from the same model, shown at once. Within the same prompt, a replay lowered an answer's chance of winning a decisive blind vote by 25.8 percentage points. The same stored text won 57% of its decisive votes when streamed and 29% when replayed, and voters called it less complete, more superficial and more often incorrect when replayed. Second, provider congestion slowed streamed answers. In 324,029 conversations, slower answers earned no detectable net credit in the vote, but a slower first exchange made visitors less likely to ask a follow-up question. Third, in 4,378,514 WildChat replies from everyday ChatGPT use, replies slowed by congestion made users less likely to continue. Delivery moved blind votes, in the direction opposite to the one the arena's designers expected, while waiting cost follow-up questions that a comparison between two answers cannot register when both are slow. The results bear on how AI services cache and stream answers, how they budget latency, and how preference leaderboards evaluate models.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Chen, Di Zhu, Lei Nico Zheng

item.title: Binding Constraints in a Strategic Technology: An Industrial Vulnerability Index for the Foundation Model Industry
item.description: arXiv:2510.23421v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Industrial policy directed at artificial intelligence has become substantial. Public investment concentrates on compute, where private capacity expansion is already underway, and is largely absent from grid interconnection and generation. Whether that allocation accurately reflects the most binding constraint in production has not yet been systematically measured. This paper introduces the Artificial Intelligence Industrial Vulnerability Index (AIIVI) as a framework for assessing potential production constraints in frontier AI. We construct a composite index of input vulnerability for the foundation model industry from fourteen concentration and sustainability parameters, aggregated by an O-Ring functional form in which capability is strongly influenced by the most constrained input. AIIVI should not be interpreted as a direct measurement of production constraints. Rather, it provides an index-based approximation derived from observable indicators and weighting assumptions designed to capture relative exposure to input vulnerabilities. Using this transparent and reproducible framework for estimating the relative vulnerability of frontier AI production to disruptions across key input dimensions, we also evaluate the index at 31 August 2026 for the nine developers at the capability frontier. We find values of 0.75 under AI-elicited weights and 0.62 under equal weights. The analysis identifies compute and energy as the principal drivers of input vulnerability. Marginal changes in these dimensions produce substantially larger variations in AIIVI than comparable changes in capital, talent, or data. We highlight three exposures that receive limited attention in existing assessment frameworks: the increasing reliance on external debt for data-centre financing, local opposition as a constraint on data-centre siting, and export controls targeting deployed AI models rather than hardware.
item.dc:creator: Claudio Pirrone, Stefano Fricano, Gioacchino Fazio

item.title: Demand Models for Market-Level Data with Closed-Form Inverses
item.description: arXiv:2610.10069v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a class of demand models for market-level data. The models can be estimated by linear instrumental variables regression while accommodating substitution patterns far richer than the logit and nested logit models they embed. They are built from closed-form inverse market share functions through a generator analogous to McFadden's generalized extreme value generating function, but acting on market shares. Constructive results allow arbitrary nesting structures, including overlapping nests and partial membership, yielding inverse-share analogs of generalized extreme value models. The class is consistent with utility maximization and strictly larger than the class of regular additive random utility models.
item.dc:creator: Julien Monardo, Mogens Fosgerau, Andr\'e de Palma

item.title: Stay, Reposition, or Recharge: Battery-Aware Operation of Robotaxi Fleets
item.description: arXiv:2611.07699v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electric robotaxis are rapidly expanding from pilots to scaled commercial deployment; unlike traditional human-driven ride-hailing vehicles, they require centralized fleet control and careful management of vehicle state of charge (SoC). We study how a fleet manager should jointly make service, empty repositioning, idling, and charging decisions in such systems. We develop a continuous-time fluid model in which vehicles evolve across location-charge states, and identify two forms of charge-aware control that are absent from classic repositioning models: early return-to-depot (RTD) and charge-aware repositioning. In particular, the optimal solution admits simple threshold structures. Each location has a battery threshold such that vehicles should return to the depot to recharge when their SoC is below it and should not do so when their SoC is above it. Vehicles should not reposition below the same threshold either; above it, the choice of destination depends on whether a vehicle's SoC matches the destination's battery sensitivity, a notion we introduce in the paper. We then quantify the value of charge awareness by comparing fully charge-aware policies with charge-oblivious policies that ignore SoC in RTD and repositioning decisions. We show that the performance gap can be unbounded, driven by a dilemma between under-utilizing high-charge vehicles and over-sending low-charge vehicles to locations from which charging is costly. A numerical case study calibrated using 2025 NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission trip records illustrates these thresholds and shows that charge-aware control can generate substantial gains in a realistic urban network. Importantly, simple threshold-based heuristics recover most of the value of the fully charge-aware solution.
item.dc:creator: Philipp Af\`eche (Kamessi), Saif Benjaafar (Kamessi), Jiayu (Kamessi), Zhao
